title: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers
gist: Programmer-turned-writer Sheon Han argues that AI coding agents, which became 'massively, belittlingly better' at his job within a year of early-2025 CLI tools, mark not the end of programming but the end of programmers: humans are becoming operators who prompt platoons of agents, as more than 90% of code at firms like Anthropic and Coinbase is reportedly AI-written. He contends this ends programming as a craft, erodes hands-on skill, and replaces flow with a gambling-like 'machine zone', while massively increasing individual output.

insights.claim: More than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase was reported in 2026 to be written with AI, making much of modern software engineering machine-operated.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Signals that AI coding tools have reached near-total adoption at leading firms, supporting demand for coding-agent vendors and pressuring engineering headcount.
insights.quote: more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI
insights.locator: Earlier this year, it was reported

insights.claim: Sheon Han argues AI coding agents will not end programming but will end programmers, because the programming is now done by a platoon of agents while humans prompt them as operators one degree removed from the work.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Reframes the software labor market: value shifts from writing code to directing agents, reshaping hiring, wages and developer-tool demand.
insights.quote: While this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers.
insights.locator: While this may not be the end of programming

insights.claim: Han frames the change as cooks ceasing to make food and instead writing recipes, with software engineering increasingly about specifying intent in markdown files rather than writing code.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Specification and orchestration layers become the key value capture point in software development tooling.
insights.quote: as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead
insights.locator: An operator is someone a degree removed

insights.claim: Han rejects Simon Willison's table-saw analogy for LLMs, arguing that unlike carpenters with power tools, programmers who cede control over the final unit of manipulation are no longer craftspeople.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Challenges the consensus 'AI is just a better tool' narrative, implying a deeper structural change to the developer profession.
insights.quote: this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople

insights.claim: Han sees AI coding as the continuation of programming's march to higher abstraction—from bytes to assembly to Python—and is not pessimistic about engineering quality, saying tasks constitutionally unfit for the human brain have been handed off.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Suggests AI-written software quality need not degrade, supporting continued enterprise adoption.
insights.locator: This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist

insights.claim: AI command-line coding tools released in early 2025 initially offered mostly eager help, then improved gradually then suddenly, becoming massively better than the author at his programming job within a year.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Documents a rapid capability inflection in agentic coding during 2025–2026, a key datapoint for AI productivity theses.
insights.quote: Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.
insights.locator: Then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools

insights.claim: Han proposes a usefulness heuristic: if forced to choose for life between pair-programming with a competent colleague or AI coding tools, any honest programmer would choose the tools—he would pick LLMs even over Linus Torvalds.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Implies AI tools substitute for, not just complement, collaborating engineers, with headcount implications.
insights.quote: Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs
insights.locator: Some engineers still labor a great deal

insights.claim: Early ChatGPT and GPT-4 behaved like a monkey's paw for code, producing locally correct solutions that mangled the surrounding code, unlike later agentic tools.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Shows how quickly the reliability bar moved from chat assistants to agents, explaining the adoption surge.
insights.locator: I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting

insights.claim: Using Claude Code, Han built a heavyweight Scrivener-like word processor with 239 features, 17 extensions and 141 keyboard shortcuts, plus 13 iOS and Mac apps without knowing Swift syntax.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Illustrates how coding agents let individuals replace niche consumer apps, a threat to small subscription and ad-supported software.
insights.locator: Even though I’ve stopped coding myself

insights.claim: Han spent 10 hours in a single day using Claude Code and then 8 hours the next day despite resolving to cut back, likening AI coding's pull to the gambler's 'machine zone' rather than true flow.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Compulsive engagement drives heavy usage of agentic tools, supporting usage-based revenue but raising wellbeing concerns.
insights.quote: the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler
insights.locator: Another loss is that programming no longer

insights.claim: Han reports that relying on AI coding tools caused a swift and decisive decline in his own coding ability and eliminated his interest in learning new programming languages.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Skill atrophy deepens dependency on AI vendors and raises long-run risks for engineering talent pipelines.
insights.quote: my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline
insights.locator: For someone who feels no allegiance to tech

insights.claim: Han predicts there will no longer be great individual programmers in the mold of Brian W. Kernighan, coauthor of The C Programming Language.
insights.speaker: Sheon Han
insights.so_what: Individual engineering virtuosity becomes less of a differentiator, commoditizing software talent.
